readerTitle: Four calls that decide where a dumpling shop grows next
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (만두 식당의 두 번째 매장) · 배달 앱 주문 데이터라는 디지털 요소 포함 · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 좋은 성장은 한 번의 큰 결단이 아니라, 매 단계에서 검증된 것은 그대로 두고 새로운 변수를 하나씩만 늘리는 선택의 연속이다.
misconception: 가장 큰 시장이나 가장 싼 입지가 최고의 다음 시장이고, 성장하려면 한 번에 크게 걸어야 한다.

sources.text: 성장 방향 구분의 표준 개념 (Ansoff, H. I. (1957). Strategies for Diversification. Harvard Business Review)
모든 인물, 매장, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치(40석, 대기 1시간, 배달 주문의 약 5분의 1, 6개월 푸드홀 운영)는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 데이터로 오해되지 않도록 모든 시나리오 카드에 illustrative 라벨을 붙였습니다.
6번 카드의 '새 매장이 기존 매장 배달 주문을 가져가는 현상(카니발리제이션)'은 일반적인 경영 개념으로 설명했으며 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.
8번 카드의 'Next' 예고 문구는 다음 유닛 첫 레슨 제목이 확정되면 교체하세요.

cards.title: Mira's dumpling shop has a line out the door.
body: Mira runs a 40-seat dumpling restaurant. Weekend waits run an hour, and delivery orders grow every month. Her bank will lend for one growth move this year.
Over the next four cards, you make her calls. Each choice shapes the next one.

image.label: A small dumpling restaurant with a queue outside
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 만두 가게 앞에 손님 줄이 길게 서 있고, 가게 옆으로 배달 오토바이가 출발하는 장면. 가게 위에 갈림길 표지판 네 개가 희미하게 떠 있음. 실제 브랜드나 배달 앱 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which way should Mira grow?
body: Three ideas keep coming up in conversations with her staff and regulars.

options.text: Open a second dumpling restaurant in another neighborhood
options.feedback: Same menu, recipes and know-how, aimed at new customers. Only one thing changes: the place.

options.text: Launch frozen dumplings for grocery stores
options.feedback: It uses her recipes, but grocery buyers, packaging, shelf fees and food-safety rules are all new to her. That's several bets at once.

options.text: Open a burger bar next door to catch the waiting crowd
options.feedback: New product, new kitchen, new skills. It shares little with her shop except the street, and it splits her attention.

cards.title: Say you chose a second restaurant. Where?
body: Three neighborhoods are on the table.

options.text: Riverside, with the cheapest rent in town
options.feedback: Rent is often cheap for a reason, like thin foot traffic. You save on rent and may pay for it in empty tables.

options.text: Downtown, with the biggest daytime crowd
options.feedback: Lots of people, but also high rent, many rivals, and nobody who knows her name yet.

options.text: Eastgate, 20 minutes away, where about one in five of her delivery orders already go
options.feedback: Demand is already proven there. These customers know her food and have been paying for it.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams can run the same check: look at where signups, trials or paying users already come from, by country or industry, before picking a new market.

cards.title: Say you picked Eastgate. How do you get in?
body: Delivery orders prove people like her food at home. They don't prove people will come and sit down.

options.text: Sign a 10-year lease and build a full restaurant
options.feedback: Full control and the full margin. But it is her biggest bet, placed before she knows whether dine-in demand matches delivery demand.

options.text: Buy a struggling noodle shop there, with its lease and staff
options.feedback: Fast, with a kitchen ready to use. But she inherits its reputation, its staff habits and whatever made it struggle.

options.text: Run a six-month stall in Eastgate's food hall, sharing seats and kitchen
options.feedback: A cheap test of real demand, at the cost of some control and margin. If it works, she builds with evidence.

cards.title: Say the stall sold out. Now supply wobbles.
body: Mira opens a full Eastgate restaurant. Months later, her wrapper supplier misses two deliveries in one month. A retiring wrapper-factory owner offers to sell her his business.

options.text: Buy the factory and secure supply for good
options.feedback: Supply is safe, but now she runs a factory built for far more volume than two restaurants use. Cash and attention leave the restaurants.

options.text: Add a second supplier and sign contracts with delivery terms
options.feedback: She cuts the risk without owning a business she doesn't know. She pays slightly more and accepts less control.

options.text: Make wrappers by hand in both kitchens
options.feedback: Fresh and fully under her control, but it adds hours of labor at each site and makes consistency harder.

cards.title: Some of Eastgate's sales were already hers.
body: Many of the new restaurant's customers used to order delivery from the first shop. Those orders moved, they didn't grow. When you judge a new location, count only the sales that are truly new.

Tests can mislead too. A food-hall crowd is not the same as people choosing her restaurant on purpose. And each new site nearby eats a little more of the last one's area. **Close moves** are safer, but they run out sooner.

cards.title: Change one thing at a time.
body: Each best answer kept something proven. Same product, new place. Then a place where customers already knew her. Then a small test before a big lease. Then a contract instead of a factory.
Every new element is a separate bet: a new product, new customers, new skills, new assets. Bets stack up. **Good growth moves** change as few things at once as possible, and test before they commit.

image.label: A staircase where each step changes one thing
image.brief: 계단 인포그래픽. 네 칸 계단에 각각 "Same product, new place", "Where demand already is", "Test, then build", "Contract, don't own" 라벨. 옆에 한 번에 크게 뛰려다 떨어지는 작은 인물을 대비로 표시. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Grow by keeping what works and adding one new thing.
body: Each of your four calls matches an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 · Four ways to grow:** an existing product in a new market is the smallest leap
**Decision 2 · Entering new markets:** go where demand already shows
**Decision 3 · Build, buy or partner:** partner to test, build once it's proven
**Decision 4 · Vertical integration:** own your supply only when scale and risk justify it
cards.callout: **Try it today:** write down your next growth idea. List everything it changes: product, customers, skills, assets. Can you remove one change, or test one first?
